concepts.title: Props
concepts.description: Props are the read-only inputs a parent component passes down to a child, and they're the primary way components share data and communicate in a React application.
learningObjectives: Explain why props must be treated as read-only inside the component that receives them.
Predict what happens on screen when a component mutates a prop directly.
Give a prop a default value and explain exactly when that default is used.
Explain what the children prop is and how it enables composition.
Use a function passed as a prop so a child can communicate an event back up to its parent.

sections.heading: Props Flow One Way: Parent to Child
sections.body:
A **prop** is a value a parent component passes into a child, the way an argument is passed into a function. Conceptually, `<PriceTag amount={19.99} />` calls `PriceTag({ amount: 19.99 })`. So the discipline you apply to a function's parameters applies to props too: you read them, you don't reassign them and expect the caller to notice.

This matters more in React than in an ordinary function, because of what mutating a prop breaks. React's data flow is unidirectional: data moves down the component tree from parent to child, never back up through mutation. A parent owns a piece of data; it decides when that data changes and re-renders its children with the new value. If a child reaches into its props and changes them (`props.amount = props.amount * 1.1`), two things go wrong. React has no idea anything changed, since nothing called a state setter or passed new props down, so nothing gets scheduled to re-render. And the child has violated its contract with the parent, which still believes it is the sole owner of that value. (In development React freezes the props object, so that exact assignment throws a TypeError. The same idea applies to an object nested inside a prop, which is not frozen.) In a larger app, where many components may receive the same object, an out-of-band mutation like this is brutal to track down, because the data changed far from wherever the symptom shows up.

When a component needs to show something that changes over time, don't mutate the prop. Give the component its own **state** (the next concept), which it is allowed to update, or derive a new value locally (`const amountWithTax = amount * 1.1;`) instead of reassigning `amount`.

sections.heading: Default Prop Values
The children Prop and Composition
Callbacks: How a Child Talks Back to Its Parent

examples.title: Mutating a Prop vs Deriving a Local Value
examples.explanation: Both components render the same number, so the bug is easy to miss. Here `amount` is a number, so reassigning the parameter only changes a local variable. The habit is the problem: the moment the input is an object, the same instinct ("just update it in place") mutates the parent's data and becomes a hard-to-trace bug. PriceTag avoids this: it never touches `amount` and computes a separate value from it.

examples.title: children Enables Composition Without Extra Props
examples.explanation: Card is used twice with different nested content, and Card itself needs no changes: no `bodyText` prop, no `showButton` flag, no special-casing. `children` is filled in from whatever JSX is nested at each call site, and Card only decides where it goes (inside `.card-body`). A component built around children can be reused in situations its author never anticipated.

misconceptions.description: If a child component needs to update something, it should just directly change the prop value it was given, the way you'd update a local variable.
misconceptions.clarification: Mutating a prop doesn't propagate anywhere and doesn't trigger a re-render -- React only reacts to a state setter being called, or a parent passing genuinely new props down after its own re-render. The correct pattern is the reverse: the parent owns the data (usually as state) and passes the child a callback prop. The child calls it to report what happened, and the parent decides how to update its own state. The new value flows back down as a fresh prop, and the child never touches the original data.
misconceptions.fact: Mutating a prop doesn't propagate anywhere and doesn't trigger a re-render -- React only reacts to a state setter being called, or a parent passing genuinely new props down after its own re-render.

misconceptions.description: children is special React syntax you have to specifically opt into, separate from normal props.
misconceptions.clarification:
children is a completely ordinary prop, populated automatically by React with whatever's nested between a component's JSX tags. You read it like any other prop, including by destructuring (`function Card({ children })`), and you could even pass it as a named attribute (`Hi

} />`), though nesting content between tags is the more readable way. It's a prop with a reserved name and automatic population, nothing more.
misconceptions.fact: children is a completely ordinary prop, populated automatically by React with whatever's nested between a component's JSX tags.

exercises.prompt: What does each of these three calls log to the console?
hints: The default value `= "Guest"` is ordinary JavaScript default syntax, not something React-specific. What JS rule triggers it?
Does the default trigger for any falsy value, or for one particular value?
null and undefined both feel like 'nothing', but default values treat them differently. Which one counts as 'not passed'?
exercises.expectedAnswer: "Hi, Guest!", then "Hi, null!", then "Hi, Guest!". The default only applies when the value is undefined. An explicit null is used as-is (interpolated into the template string as the text "null"), while an explicit undefined, or a missing key, triggers the default.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `greet({})` has no `name` key, so destructuring sees `name` as `undefined`, which is the condition the default checks for, and `name` becomes "Guest": "Hi, Guest!". `greet({ name: null })` supplies `null`, which is not `undefined`, so the default is never used; template-string interpolation turns `null` into the text "null": "Hi, null!". `greet({ name: undefined })` supplies `undefined`, so it behaves like the first case: "Hi, Guest!". A default is a stand-in for "this value is undefined", not for any falsy or empty value, which matters whenever a prop might legitimately be `null`, `0` or `""`.

exercises.prompt: Clicking "Apply 10% off" is supposed to reduce the shown price by 10%, but nothing changes on screen (assume React only re-renders a component when its own state or props change, and this component receives no new props between clicks). Find the bug and describe a fix.
hints: item is an object prop. What's different about mutating a field on an object prop versus reassigning a primitive prop like a number or string?
item.price = ... does change the object in memory, since objects are mutated in place. So is the data wrong, or is something else not happening?
Does calling applyDiscount tell React, in any way, that it should re-run ShoppingCartItem and produce fresh JSX?
exercises.solutionExplanation: item is an object, so `item.price = item.price * 0.9` mutates the parent's own data in place. Unlike reassigning a primitive parameter, this changes the shared object for everyone holding a reference. But the mutation never goes through React: no state setter was called, so nothing schedules a re-render, and ShoppingCartItem keeps showing what it last rendered, now out of sync with the mutated price in memory. The fix removes the mutation: the child calls a callback prop (`onApplyDiscount`) that the parent supplies, and the parent, which owns the cart data, applies the discount through its own state setter (not shown, typically something like `setItems(items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, price: i.price * 0.9 } : i))`). That triggers a re-render with the new price flowing back down as a fresh prop.

assessments.prompt: A child component needs to notify its parent that the user clicked a "Delete" button, so the parent can remove that item from its list. What is the standard React way to do this?
options: The child imports the parent's state setter function directly and calls it.
The parent passes a callback function down as a prop (e.g. onDelete).
The child directly sets props.onDelete = true, and the parent checks that prop on its next render.
The child mutates a shared global variable that the parent happens to also read.
assessments.explanation: Data flows one way in React, parent to child, so a child can't reach up and modify something the parent owns. The standard mechanism is for the parent to pass a function as a prop; the child calls it (typically from an event handler) to report that something happened, and the parent decides what to do, usually by updating its own state. The “The child directly sets props.onDelete = true…” option describes mutating a prop, which doesn't propagate anywhere and triggers no re-render. The “The child imports the parent's state setter…” option isn't how components are structured: a child doesn't import a parent's internal state setter; it only receives what the parent hands it as a prop. The “The child mutates a shared global variable…” option describes an ad hoc global-mutation pattern that defeats React's data-flow model and its ability to know when to re-render.

options: 0 (the number), because the default parameter mechanism only triggers when the value is exactly undefined, not for any other falsy value like 0.
undefined, because 0 is not considered a valid value to pass as a prop.
"primary", because 0 is falsy, so the default parameter kicks in.
"" (an empty string), because React coerces unusual prop values to an empty string before passing them along.
assessments.explanation: A prop's default, written with ordinary JavaScript default syntax, only applies when the value is undefined, not for other falsy values. Here variant is the number 0, a defined value that happens to be falsy, so the default "primary" is never used. variant stays 0 inside Button, and className={variant} gets that number, not "primary". This is the rule that trips people up when they assume 'falsy means use the default.'

options: The literal string "children".
undefined, since children was never explicitly passed as an attribute like children={...}.
A React element (or set of elements) representing everything nested between <Alert> and </Alert> -- here, the <strong> element and the surrounding text -- automatically populated by React.
An empty array, since Alert never declared a specific children prop type or shape.
assessments.explanation: children is an ordinary prop, not special syntax: React fills it with whatever JSX is nested between a component's opening and closing tags. Here that's the Warning: element plus the text "Disk space low.", available to Alert as props.children (destructured as children). Alert doesn't opt in beyond reading the prop, and passing it as an attribute (children={...}) would work identically.

concepts.title: State
concepts.description: State is data a component owns itself, can change over its lifetime, and -- unlike a prop or a plain local variable -- persists across re-renders and must be updated through a setter so React knows to re-render.
learningObjectives: Explain how state differs from props: who owns it, and what triggers it to change.
Explain why directly mutating a state value (e.g. state.value = x) does not cause a re-render.
Explain, in terms of what React can and can't observe, why a setter function is required.
Predict whether a given value persists across re-renders based on whether it's state or a plain local variable.
Apply the principle of state colocation to decide where a piece of state should live.

sections.heading: State vs Props: Who Owns What
Why Direct Mutation Doesn't Trigger a Re-render
sections.body:
The first rule of state in React: **writing directly to a state value (`state.value = x`, or mutating an object or array stored in state) does not cause a re-render.** You must call the setter function React gave you.

The reason is worth understanding rather than memorizing. JavaScript has no general-purpose way to 'watch' a plain variable or an object's property and be notified when it changes, so React can't observe every value in your program for mutations. A function component is a function that gets called again to produce new output, and React decides *when* to call it again based on a small set of triggers: a state setter being called, or a parent re-rendering and passing new props. If you mutate state directly, the value may well change in memory (for an object, the mutation persists), but you didn't go through a trigger React watches, so nothing tells React to call the component again. The screen keeps showing what it last rendered, out of sync with the data in memory.

The setter is the mechanism, not a formality: `setCount(newValue)` means both 'store this as the current value' and 'schedule a re-render.' Note that the new value shows up on the *next* render, not inside the handler that called the setter: within one render, `count` is a fixed snapshot. So `setCount(count + 1)` called three times in one handler adds 1, not 3, because each call sees the same `count`. When the new value depends on the previous one, pass an updater function (`setCount((c) => c + 1)`), which React applies in order.

sections.heading: Mutating an Object in State: The Same Bug, More Deceptive
State Persists Across Renders, a Local Variable Doesn't
sections.body: State also differs from a plain variable declared in the component's function body, in a way that has nothing to do with mutation. Every render calls the component function again from scratch, so any `let` or `const` in the body is recreated from its initial value on every render. State isn't: React stores it separately, associated with this component instance, outside any one call to the function. Calling `useState(0)` on the fifth render does not reset the value to `0`; the `0` is only used on the first render for that instance, and every render after that, `useState` returns whatever was most recently set. That is why state needs a hook at all: an ordinary variable can't survive the whole function rerunning from the top. One more thing you may notice while experimenting: in development, `<StrictMode>` renders each component twice to expose impure rendering, so a `console.log` placed in the component body prints twice. That is expected, only happens in development, and is another reason to keep render free of side effects such as mutating variables outside the component; handlers like the click handlers above run once per event.

sections.heading: State Colocation: Keep State Close to Where It's Used
sections.body:
A design principle follows from 'state is owned by whichever component holds it': put a piece of state in the lowest component that needs it, not higher up 'just in case.' If only one component reads and updates a value, it should live in that component. Hoisting it to a parent ahead of time gains nothing.

The exception is when two or more sibling components need the *same* value, such as a search box and a results list that both depend on the current query text. The state then has to move up to the nearest common ancestor of the siblings (called **lifting state up**, covered as its own concept later), since neither sibling can hold state the other must see. Do that in response to a real sharing requirement, not by default: state kept unnecessarily high makes more of the tree re-render and forces you to pass the value through components that don't care about it. Start local; lift when you have to.

examples.title: A Plain Local Variable vs Real State
examples.explanation: In BrokenCounter, `count` is a plain local variable, recreated by `let count = 0` every time the function runs. Clicking does increment it (the console.log shows that), but nothing calls BrokenCounter again, so the button stays at "Clicked 0 times". Even if something else caused a re-render, `let count = 0` would reset it to 0. Counter asks React to own the value via useState: `count` survives across renders (tied to the component instance, not to one function call), and `setCount(...)` updates the stored value and schedules the re-render that shows it.

examples.title: Mutating Object State Fails Without an Error
examples.explanation: haveBirthdayBroken changes `user.age` in memory, but since it never calls `setUser`, React never learns anything happened, so the paragraph keeps showing the old age. haveBirthdayFixed builds a new object with the spread operator and passes it to `setUser`. That is a call to the setter (which schedules the re-render) with a fresh reference, which is what state updates for objects and arrays should look like: never mutate the existing value, produce a new one and hand it to the setter. (The component has no button wired to either handler; imagine an onClick calling one of them.)

misconceptions.description: If I mutate an object or array stored in state, React should notice, since the underlying data really did change.
misconceptions.clarification: React schedules a re-render when the setter returned by useState is called; it never inspects the value it's holding to detect that something inside changed. Mutating an object in place does change it in memory, but bypasses the setter call React relies on. The fix is to call the setter with a new value (a copied-and-modified object or array) instead of mutating the existing one.

misconceptions.description: State gets reset every time the component re-renders, the same way a plain local variable declared in the function body would.
misconceptions.clarification: This is backwards. A plain local variable IS reset every render, because the function body runs again from scratch. State isn't: React stores it outside any single function call, tied to the component instance, and on later renders useState(initialValue) ignores initialValue and returns whatever was most recently set. State resets only when the component instance unmounts and a fresh one mounts later (or when its key changes); a render on its own never resets it.

exercises.prompt: The button below is clicked three times. What text does the page actually display after all three clicks, and what does each of the three console.log lines print?
hints: `let plainCount = 0;` sits at the top of the component's function body. When does that line run?
Every re-render calls Counters from the top again. What happens to a `let` declaration at the top of a function each time the function runs?
stateCount is different: useState only uses its argument (0) on the very first render for this component instance, and otherwise returns whatever was most recently set via setStateCount.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The page shows "Plain: 0 | State: 3" after three clicks: Plain never advances past 0, while State climbs to 3. All three console.log lines print "plainCount: 1" (never a running total), paired with the stateCount from the render each click's handleClick closed over: 0, then 1, then 2.
exercises.solutionExplanation: plainCount is re-declared by `let plainCount = 0` every time Counters runs, and Counters runs again on every re-render. Each click's handleClick increments its own render's plainCount to 1, but that increment doesn't survive: the next render starts with plainCount at 0 again before anything is displayed. So the JSX always shows "Plain: 0". React persists stateCount across renders, so each click's setStateCount(stateCount + 1) advances the stored value by one and the displayed State climbs 0, 1, 2, 3. The console.log lines show the closure mechanics: each handleClick was created during a specific render and closes over that render's plainCount (0 before the increment, 1 after) and that render's stateCount (0 on the first click, 1 on the second, 2 on the third). They are one step behind the value setStateCount is storing, because the component hasn't re-rendered yet when console.log runs inside the same handler call.

exercises.prompt: Clicking a to-do item is supposed to toggle its strikethrough (done) styling, but clicking any item does nothing: nothing re-renders and no console error appears. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: setTodos IS being called here, so why might React still skip the re-render? Think about the value being passed to it.
`todos` is the same array reference before and after `todo.done = !todo.done` runs: mutating an item inside an array doesn't change the array's identity.
React compares the new state value to the old one to decide whether anything changed. What does that comparison give when you pass back the same reference?
exercises.solutionExplanation: toggleDone mutates `todo.done` in place and then calls `setTodos(todos)`, but `todos` is the same array reference as before; only its contents changed. React compares the new state to the old with `Object.is`, and since the array passed to setTodos is the object already stored, React concludes nothing changed and skips the re-render. The screen doesn't update even though the data was mutated. The fix avoids mutation: `.map()` builds a new array, and for the matching to-do a new object (`{ ...t, done: !t.done }`). The new array is a different reference, so React detects the change and re-renders. Nothing was mutated in place, which also protects other code holding references to the same objects.

assessments.prompt: A component has `const [items, setItems] = useState([1, 2, 3]);` and a click handler that calls `items.push(4);`. Why doesn't the UI update to show the new item?
options: Because arrays can't be stored in state at all -- only primitive values like numbers and strings can.
Because push() throws an error inside React components, so the update never actually happens.
Because push() is asynchronous, so the update simply hasn't finished by the time the component re-renders.
Because React only schedules a re-render when its setter function (here, setItems) is called.
assessments.explanation: push() runs fine and does mutate the array in memory; the data changed, but React never finds out. React schedules a re-render when the state setter is called; it doesn't watch the contents of the value it's holding. Since setItems was never called, the component keeps showing what it last rendered, out of sync with the mutated array. The “Because push() throws an error inside React…” option is false: push() works fine on a plain array, React or not. The “Because arrays can't be stored in state…” option is false: arrays and objects are common things to store in state; the issue is mutation, not the type of value. The “Because push() is asynchronous, so the update…” option misdescribes push(), which is synchronous; the issue is that no setter call occurred to trigger a re-render.

options: count becomes undefined after the first re-render, since useState is only reliable on a component's initial render.

count keeps whatever value it was last set to (0, since setCount is never called here) -- React ignores the 0 argument to useState on every render after the very first one, for as long as this component instance stays mounted.
count automatically updates to match refreshKey on every re-render, since refreshKey changing is itself a kind of state update.
count resets back to 0 on every single re-render, since useState(0) runs again on each call to Widget.
assessments.explanation: React associates state with a component instance, not with a single call to the component function. The 0 passed to useState(0) initializes the state the first time this instance renders. Re-rendering Widget with a new refreshKey prop doesn't unmount or remount it, so each later call to useState(0) returns the current count and ignores the 0. Nothing calls setCount, so count stays at 0 through every re-render; new props have no effect on state that nothing has updated.

assessments.prompt: A SearchBox component and a ResultsList component are rendered as siblings inside one App component. Both need the same searchTerm value: SearchBox updates it as the user types, and ResultsList reads it to filter what it displays. Where should searchTerm's state most appropriately live?
options: Inside SearchBox only, since it's the component whose input actually updates the value.
Independently inside each of SearchBox and ResultsList, with some mechanism keeping the two copies automatically synchronized.
In the nearest common ancestor of both components -- App.
Inside ResultsList only, since it's the component that actually needs to read the value to filter its output.
assessments.explanation: The default is to keep state as low and local as possible, which only works cleanly when one component needs it. Here two siblings need the same value, one to update it and one to read it, and neither can hold state the other must see, since state only flows down from where it's declared. So lift the state to the nearest common ancestor (App), which passes searchTerm down to ResultsList as a prop and passes searchTerm and a setter (or an onChange-style callback) down to SearchBox. That keeps a single source of truth instead of two copies to keep in sync.

concepts.title: Events and Forms
concepts.description: React normalizes DOM events into a consistent synthetic event system, and forms are typically built as controlled inputs where state drives what the input displays and every keystroke updates that state.
learningObjectives: Explain what React's synthetic event system is and why it exists, at a practical level.
Build a controlled input where an input's displayed value comes from state.
Explain what makes an input 'uncontrolled' and diagnose the classic 'my input won't let me type' bug.
Explain why e.preventDefault() is almost always needed inside a React onSubmit handler.
Predict the consequence of forgetting preventDefault() on a form submission.

sections.heading: React's Synthetic Event System
sections.body: When you write `onClick={handleClick}` or `onChange={handleChange}` in JSX, you're using React's **synthetic event system**: React wraps the browser's native event objects in its own wrapper before handing them to your handler. You don't need the internals to use it. What matters is that event props like `onClick`, `onChange` and `onSubmit` exist for the interactions you'd expect, they're named in camelCase like other JSX attributes, and the event object your handler receives (`e` or `event`, by convention, as the first argument) behaves the same across browsers. React attaches and cleans up the underlying listeners for you, so you don't call `addEventListener` for ordinary clicks or input changes. One difference from plain JavaScript: React's `onChange` on a text input fires on every keystroke, like the native `input` event, whereas the native `change` event fires when the field loses focus. Pass the function itself, not a call to it: `onClick={handleClick}` registers a handler, while `onClick={handleClick()}` runs `handleClick` during rendering and passes its return value. When you need to pass an argument, wrap the call in an arrow function: `onClick={() => handleDelete(item.id)}`.

sections.heading: Controlled Inputs: State Drives the DOM
Controlled vs Uncontrolled: The Missing value Prop
sections.body:
An input is **uncontrolled** when it's rendered without a `value` prop bound to state, for example `<input onChange={handleChange} />` with no `value=`. The DOM is then the source of truth for what's typed, not React. That's a legitimate, if less common, choice (typically combined with `defaultValue` and a ref, or read from `FormData` on submit), useful for very large forms where controlling every keystroke would be wasteful.

The more common case is doing this *by accident*: writing `<input value={text} />` with no `onChange` handler. React warns about a `value` without an `onChange`, and the input can't be typed into. On every keystroke the DOM tries to update its display, but after the event React sets the DOM value back to the `value` prop, and `text` never changed because nothing called a setter. The input snaps back to its old contents on every keypress. 'My input won't let me type anything' is one of the most common beginner bugs in React, and it almost always traces back to a `value` prop with no matching `onChange`.

sections.heading: Handling Form Submission: onSubmit and preventDefault

examples.title: A Controlled Text Input
examples.explanation:
The input's text and the `

` below it both reflect the `name` state variable. Typing a character fires onChange, which reads `e.target.value` (the input's new content) and stores it via setName, triggering a re-render where the input's value prop and the paragraph both show the updated state. Nothing reads the DOM's value independently; state is the single source of truth.

examples.title: A Form With preventDefault
examples.explanation: Both fields are controlled inputs feeding their own state. handleSubmit's first line, e.preventDefault(), stops the browser's default full-page navigation that would otherwise follow the submission (whether by clicking the button or pressing Enter in a field). Without it the console.log would still run, but the page would then reload, wiping the state and, unless the console's 'Preserve log' option is on, the log itself.

misconceptions.description: You need to call addEventListener manually inside a component to listen for clicks or input changes, the same way you would in plain JavaScript.
misconceptions.clarification: JSX event props like onClick and onChange wire this up declaratively: React attaches (and later cleans up) the underlying event listeners for you. You supply the handler as a prop, with no addEventListener/removeEventListener bookkeeping for ordinary interactions.

misconceptions.description: An input with its value prop bound to state but no onChange handler is a perfectly valid way to make a kind of 'read-only-looking' controlled input.
misconceptions.clarification: This produces a React warning (a value prop without an onChange handler) and an input the user can't type into: each keystroke's visual change is overwritten with the unchanged state value, since nothing called a setter. For a read-only field, use the `readOnly` attribute (`<input value={text} readOnly />`) instead of omitting onChange.

exercises.prompt: What happens when a user clicks into this input and tries to type the word "react"?
hints: The input's value prop is bound to query state. Does anything here ever change query?
On every keystroke the browser tries to update what the input shows. What does React do with the value prop afterwards?
Compare with a controlled input that DOES have an onChange handler wired to a setter. What's missing here?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Nothing appears to get typed: the input rejects every keystroke and stays empty (query never leaves its initial value of ""), and React logs a console warning about a value prop without an onChange handler.
exercises.solutionExplanation: value={query} makes this a controlled input, so React (not the DOM) is the source of truth for what it displays. With no onChange handler, nothing calls setQuery, so query stays "". On every keystroke the browser briefly tries to show the typed character, but React re-asserts value={query}, which is still "", and the input snaps back to empty. It looks like the input rejects all typing. This is the classic cause of 'my input won't let me type': a value prop bound to state with no onChange to update that state.

exercises.prompt: Submitting this feedback form is supposed to just log the message to the console, but instead the whole page visibly reloads/flashes and the typed message disappears. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: handleSubmit doesn't accept any parameter. What does React pass as the first argument to an onSubmit handler, and what method does that object have?
What does a browser do by default when a <form> is submitted, if nothing tells it otherwise?
Near the top of handleSubmit, one method call is missing.
exercises.solutionExplanation: handleSubmit never receives the submit event or calls preventDefault on it, so nothing stops the browser's default for a form submission, which is to navigate or reload the page. The reload wipes out the component's state, including the typed message, and to the user the page flashed and reset for no reason. The console.log does run first, but its output disappears with the reload unless the console preserves logs. The fix is to accept the event as a parameter and call e.preventDefault() as the first line, which stops the navigation and leaves handleSubmit in control.

assessments.prompt: Why does a React onSubmit handler almost always start with e.preventDefault()?
options: Because preventDefault() is required to make the form's onChange handlers fire correctly.
Because React batches state updates, and preventDefault() is what triggers that batching to actually apply.
Because JSX forms don't work at all unless preventDefault() is called first.
Because a browser's default behavior for a form submission is to navigate the page.
assessments.explanation: A <form> submission's native browser behavior is a page navigation (a reload of the current page, by default). In a React app that would tear down the component tree and its state, which you almost never want, since the app handles the submission in JavaScript. preventDefault() stops that navigation so your handler's logic (reading state, validating it, sending a request) runs without the page going away. The “Because JSX forms don't work at all…” option is false: forms render and work without it, but you also get an unwanted page navigation. The “Because preventDefault() is required to make…” option confuses submission with the separate onChange handlers on individual inputs, which fire regardless. The “Because React batches state updates, and preventDefault()…” option misattributes batching, which is an unrelated React scheduling behavior, not something preventDefault controls.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes React's synthetic event system, as used when you write `<input onChange={handleChange} />` in JSX?
options: React wraps native browser events in its own consistent wrapper, and event props like onClick/onChange/onSubmit let you attach handlers declaratively.
The synthetic event system replaces the DOM entirely, so no actual native browser event occurs underneath a React event handler.
Synthetic events only exist for onClick; typing-related interactions like onChange still require raw DOM event listeners set up separately.
You still need to manually call addEventListener and removeEventListener yourself for each JSX event prop you use; onChange is just a naming convention.
assessments.explanation: React's synthetic event system lets you declare handlers via camelCase JSX props (onClick, onChange, onSubmit, and so on) without calling addEventListener or removeEventListener yourself; React wires up (and later cleans up) the underlying listeners. The “You still need to manually call addEventListener…” option describes the manual bookkeeping this system removes. The “Synthetic events only exist for onClick; typing-related…” option is false: onChange, onSubmit and the other standard event props all work the same declarative way. The “The synthetic event system replaces the DOM…” option is false: a native browser event still happens underneath; React's synthetic event is a wrapper around it, not a replacement.

concepts.title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
concepts.description: React has a few common idioms for rendering something conditionally or rendering a collection with .map(), and both come with easy-to-hit pitfalls: a falsy-but-non-boolean short-circuit value rendering as visible text, and unstable keys causing state to attach to the wrong list item.
learningObjectives: Use ternaries, && short-circuiting, and early returns to conditionally render JSX.
Predict when a && expression renders a stray, visible value instead of nothing.
Render a list of components from an array using .map(), with a stable key on each item.
Explain, in terms of reconciliation, why React needs keys to reliably update a list.
Explain concretely what breaks when array index is used as a key for a list that can reorder or have items inserted/removed.

sections.heading: Common Conditional Rendering Patterns
sections.body: React has no special conditional-rendering syntax; you choose, with ordinary JavaScript, which JSX expression to produce. Three patterns cover almost every case: a **ternary** for either/or choices (`isLoggedIn ? <Dashboard /> : <LoginForm />`); **&& short-circuiting** for 'render this, or render nothing' (`isNewUser && <WelcomeBanner />`); and an **early return** when the whole component should render something else, most commonly for loading or error states (`if (loading) return <Spinner />;` before the main return statement). Early return is often the clearest once a component has more than one condition, since several ternaries or &&s inside one JSX return get hard to read quickly. Two details: to render nothing from a ternary branch or an early return, use `null` (`return null;` is valid and renders nothing), and put early returns *after* any hook calls such as `useState`, because hooks must run in the same order on every render.

sections.heading: The 0 && Gotcha
Rendering Lists with .map()
Why Keys Matter: Reconciliation
sections.body: Note the `key={todo.id}` above. **Keys** are how React matches each element in a newly rendered list to the corresponding element from the *previous* render, so it can decide what to do to the real DOM: update a node in place, move it, create one, or remove one that's gone. Without a stable key (or with duplicate or unstable ones), React can't tell 'the same item, now in a different position' from 'a new item that looks similar'. Getting that wrong can mean recreating DOM nodes needlessly or, worse, reusing a DOM node (and any state tied to it) for a different item than the one it used to represent. Without any key, React falls back to position and logs a warning. Keys also shouldn't be generated during render (`key={Math.random()}` gives every item a new identity on every render, so React destroys and recreates every row and its state each time). Use an id that comes with the data, or assign one when the item is created. The `key` is read by React and isn't passed to your component as a prop.

sections.heading: The Index-as-Key Anti-Pattern
sections.body:
A tempting shortcut is `key={index}` from `.map((item, index) => ...)`. It's unique within a single render, so React doesn't warn. But uniqueness within one render isn't the requirement: a key must stay attached to the *same logical item* across renders as the list changes, and an index fails that as soon as the list can reorder, or have items inserted or removed anywhere but the end.

Imagine a to-do list where each `<li>` has an uncontrolled checkbox (`<input type="checkbox" defaultChecked={todo.done} />`) keyed by index. Delete the first to-do, and every remaining to-do shifts up one position. React sees `key={0}` still present and assumes the `<li>` at position 0 is the *same* one as before, so it reuses that DOM node, including the checked state the user clicked into it, instead of the state of the to-do now sitting there. The checkbox's state ends up pinned to a *list position* rather than to the to-do, so after a deletion checkmarks can jump onto the wrong items. Keying by something that identifies the data itself (`key={todo.id}`) fixes this: React can tell which `<li>` belongs to which to-do wherever it sits in the array, so it removes only the DOM node of the deleted item and leaves every other row's node, and its state, attached to the right item.

examples.title: The 0 && Gotcha, Rendered
examples.explanation: With itemCount = 0, CartBadge's `0 && ...` evaluates to 0 (the operand && landed on), and React renders that number as text, so a stray "0" shows up exactly when the cart is empty. FixedCartBadge evaluates `itemCount > 0` first, which is a boolean (false when itemCount is 0); `false && ...` short-circuits to false, and React renders false as nothing.

examples.title: Index-as-Key Attaches State to the Wrong Row After a Reorder
examples.explanation: In PlayerList, clicking 'Sort alphabetically' reorders the players array but each <li>'s key is still its position (0, 1, 2...). React sees the same keys before and after the sort, so it treats each <li> as unchanged and reuses its DOM node, including the checkbox's live checked state, which lives in the DOM node once the user has clicked it (defaultChecked only sets the *initial* value). A checkbox that was checked for 'Zoe' can end up checked for whoever the sort places at that position. FixedPlayerList keys by player.id, so React recognizes each row across the reorder and moves the right DOM nodes (checkbox state included) with the right players. (The sort handler itself is left to the parent.)

misconceptions.description: Using the array index as a key is basically always fine, since .map((item, index) => ...) does give every item a unique key.
misconceptions.clarification: Uniqueness within a single render isn't the actual requirement -- a key needs to stay attached to the same logical item across renders, including when the list is reordered or items are inserted/removed anywhere but the end. An index identifies the same item only if the item never changes position, which fails once the list can reorder or change in the middle. A value from the data itself (an id) stays correct regardless of position.
misconceptions.fact: Uniqueness within a single render isn't the actual requirement -- a key needs to stay attached to the same logical item across renders, including when the list is reordered or items are inserted/removed anywhere but the end.

misconceptions.description: {value && <Component />} is a generally safe way to conditionally render, no matter what value actually is.
misconceptions.clarification: It's only safe when value is already a boolean, or null/undefined, which also render as nothing. If value can be the number 0 (or NaN), && returns it and React renders it as visible text. An empty string is falsy too but renders as nothing, so it's harmless here. Producing a boolean (value > 0, or Boolean(value)) avoids the surprise.

exercises.prompt: This component is rendered with unreadCount equal to 0. What actually appears on the page?
hints: What does `unreadCount && ...` evaluate to when unreadCount is 0? Not what you intend it to mean, but what JavaScript's && operator returns.
React renders certain 'nothing' values (false, null, undefined) as nothing at all on screen. Does it treat every falsy value the same way?
Try substituting 0 directly into the && expression by hand and see what value comes out the other side.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The page shows the "Inbox" heading followed by a stray "0", not nothing. Because unreadCount is 0, `unreadCount && ...` evaluates to 0 itself (not false), and React renders that literal 0 as text.
exercises.solutionExplanation: && returns whichever operand it short-circuits on, without converting it to a boolean. Since unreadCount is 0 (falsy), the expression evaluates to 0, not false. React renders numbers as text, like strings, so the 0 appears right after the Inbox heading and the page reads something like "Inbox 0" instead of just "Inbox". Rewriting the condition as `unreadCount > 0 && ...` avoids this, since a comparison always produces a boolean, and `false && ...` renders as nothing.

exercises.prompt: Each player row has its own note field (a local text input). Typing a note next to "Zoe", then clicking "Sort alphabetically", causes the typed note to visually end up attached to a different player instead of staying with Zoe. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: PlayerRow owns its own note state. React decides whether to reuse an existing component instance (state included) or discard it and mount a new one based on the key at that position.
After the sort, does key={index} still identify 'the row for Zoe,' or does it just identify 'whichever player is now third in the array'?
What would key={player.id} (or another value drawn from the player's own data) tell React that key={index} can't?
exercises.solutionExplanation: key={index} tells React 'the <li> (and the PlayerRow instance inside it) at this position is the same one as before,' which is only true if the array's order never changes. Sorting rearranges the players array, so Zoe, who was at position 4, may now be at position 1. Matching on the key (the index), React assumes the PlayerRow at position 1 is unchanged and reuses that instance and its note state instead of mounting a fresh one for the player now there. The note typed for Zoe stays attached to a list position, not to Zoe. With key={player.id}, React can tell that a PlayerRow instance belongs to a specific player wherever that player sits in the array, so it moves the right instance (and its note state) with the right player during the reorder.

assessments.prompt: Why does React need a key on each item when rendering a list with .map(), rather than just using each element's position in the array automatically?
options: Keys are required by JSX syntax rules and would cause a build error if omitted, similar to a missing closing tag.

Keys let React match each element in the new render to the corresponding element from the previous render, so it can correctly decide what to update in place, move, create, or remove -- without a stable key, it can't reliably tell 'the same item, moved' from 'a new item.'
Keys are purely a performance hint that make rendering marginally faster, but every list works identically correctly without them.
Keys determine the order elements are displayed on screen, overriding the order of the array itself.
assessments.explanation: Keys give React a stable identity for each item across renders, which makes correct reconciliation possible: telling 'this item moved from position 2 to position 0' from 'this is a new item' and 'this item was removed.' The “Keys are purely a performance hint…” option undersells the issue: without stable keys React can make the wrong call about what changed, which causes bugs (state or DOM attaching to the wrong item), not just a performance cost. The “Keys are required by JSX syntax rules…” option is false: omitting keys produces a console warning, not a build error, and the list still renders (with reconciliation correctness at risk). The “Keys determine the order elements are displayed…” option is false: the array's own order (as produced by .map()) determines display order; keys match identity across renders and don't affect sequence.

assessments.prompt: A list of checkboxes is rendered with `key={index}` from `.map((item, index) => ...)`. A new item is inserted at the very front of the array, shifting every existing item down by one position, and the list re-renders. What happens to the existing checkboxes' visual checked state?
options: Because keys are matched purely by position rather than by item identity, the checked states end up shifted.
React detects that the array's length changed and automatically remounts every item from scratch with fresh, unchecked checkboxes.
Nothing changes visually, since defaultChecked only sets the initial value and is never reconsidered after an item's very first render anyway.
Each checkbox correctly keeps the checked state of the same underlying item it originally represented, since key={index} is recalculated fresh on every render.
assessments.explanation: React reconciles a list by matching keys between the previous render and the new one; the key is its only way to tell 'same item, moved' from 'a different item that happens to be here now'. With key={index}, inserting an item at the front doesn't change the key values from React's point of view: position 0's key is still 0, position 1's is still 1, and so on. React assumes the element at each position is the one that was there before and reuses those DOM nodes, checkbox state included, for whatever item now occupies the position, even though every existing item shifted down by one. The checked states end up on the wrong items, off by one row, the same bug the concept describes for deletions and reordering.
